candidate.answerReason: Positive integer side lengths must sum to 25. The smallest area is 1×24=24 and the largest is 12×13=156, giving a difference of 132 square units.

methods.label: Method 1: List the possible side lengths
methods.explanation:
A rectangle's perimeter is twice the sum of its two different side lengths, so those lengths must sum to \(50\div2=25\). Both lengths must be positive integers.

Call the smaller side \(s\). Then the other side is \(25-s\), and \(s\) can be any integer from \(1\) through \(12\). This includes every possible rectangle; choosing the smaller side avoids listing the same pair in reverse order.

For \(s=1,2,\ldots,12\), respectively, the areas \(s(25-s)\) are
\[
\begin{gathered}
24,\ 46,\ 66,\ 84,\ 100,\ 114,\\
126,\ 136,\ 144,\ 150,\ 154,\ 156.
\end{gathered}
\]
Thus the smallest area is \(24\), attained by sides \(1\) and \(24\), and the largest is \(156\), attained by sides \(12\) and \(13\). Their difference is
\[
156-24=132\text{ square units},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
methods.levelReason: There are only twelve side pairs to check, so exhaustive elementary arithmetic proves both extrema.

methods.label: Method 2: Compare areas while balancing the sides
methods.explanation:
Let \(a\le b\) be the positive integer side lengths. The perimeter condition gives \(a+b=25\). Starting with \((1,24)\), repeatedly increase the smaller side by \(1\) and decrease the larger side by \(1\). This visits every possible side pair, ending at \((12,13)\).

Before reaching the last pair, \(b-a\ge3\). Shortening the side of length \(b\) by \(1\) removes a strip of area \(a\). Then increasing the side of length \(a\) by \(1\) adds a strip of area \(b-1\). Thus the net area increase is
\[
(b-1)-a=b-a-1\ge2>0.
\]
Every move increases the area, so the first pair gives the smallest area and the last pair gives the largest. Their difference is
\[
12\times13-1\times24=156-24=132.
\]
The answer is \(132\) square units, choice \(\mathrm{D}\).
methods.levelReason: The comparison follows from unit-strip areas and whole-number subtraction, without quadratic functions or an inequality theorem.

candidate.annotationRationale: Both methods establish universal area bounds and exhibit allowed rectangles attaining them. The perimeter formula is shared supporting knowledge. The first method exhausts all twelve side pairs; the second proves that successive balancing moves increase area, so comparison by subtraction is local to that alternative.

review.mathematicalCheck: Positive integer sides sum to 25, giving exactly the twelve listed pairs. Their areas range from 24 to 156. Independently, each balancing move increases area by b-a-1>0 until (12,13), establishing the same extrema and difference 132.
review.levelCheck: Enumeration and the unit-strip argument both use elementary geometry and arithmetic suitable for AMC 8.
review.methodDistinctness: Exhaustive enumeration and the structural balancing argument provide distinct, accessible proofs.
review.annotationCheck: Both methods establish attained universal extrema and use rectangle area and perimeter. Comparison by subtraction is correctly local to the balancing method.
